meta.title: Keepance — Board Dashboard
meta.subtitle: The private intelligence layer for a law practice
meta.framing: Jameson = Board of Directors  ·  Claude = CEO reporting in
meta.headline: One honest truth runs through everything below: Keepance is a finished, well-built product with essentially zero customers. The job now is distribution and trust — getting in front of lawyers and earning their belief — not building more.
meta.updateRule: High bar: a Claude session only updates this for a MAJOR decision, a validated insight, a strategy shift, or a real milestone. Routine work never touches it. Jameson maintains it freely.

sections.title: Strategy & Vision
sections.now: Keepance is sharpened from a general 'private AI workspace' into one clear identity: the private intelligence layer for a law practice — a desktop app where a lawyer's documents, email, and matters live on their own machine, stay private by design, and answer questions back with citations they can click and verify. The lead audience is deliberately narrow: solo and small-firm litigation lawyers first. The product vision itself is essentially complete and shipped.
decisions: Repositioned to law-first (2026-06-09): one audience, one job — 'find anything across a matter with a citation you can click.'
Sequencing (2026-06-17): finish the product vision first, then run the whole 'go sell it' reorientation as one block. Lead niche locked as litigation solo/small-firm.
The reorientation was actually executed (2026-06-17): fixed honesty problems in the product's claims, made the privacy story visible, hardened the AI against confident-but-wrong answers.
insights: Two independent reviews (one engineering, one strategic) landed on the same conclusion the same day: the #1 priority is being trustworthy and being found, not adding features.
The core thesis ('lawyers will pay for local-first private AI') is real but a tiebreaker, not a category-killer — and slowly narrowing as cloud rivals add their own privacy features.

Open board question: set a kill-criterion — a fixed window of hand-selling to lawyers, with an honest agreement that no customers + no testimonials may mean pivot (to accountants) or accept it as a small lifestyle business.

Honest tension to protect: 'nothing leaves your machine' is fully true only in the slower local-AI mode; the recommended higher-quality mode sends data to the lawyer's own AI provider. The product already frames this honestly as a privacy spectrum.

sections.title: Marketing
sections.now: There is a large, well-organized marketing library — channel playbooks, email sequences, press kit, comparison pages, battlecards — but almost none of it is currently driving traffic. The website drew ~225 visitors over a recent ten-week stretch, nearly all typing the address in directly, meaning search, social, and referrals send almost nobody. Channels were re-pointed (2026-05-27) away from startup/tech sites toward where lawyers actually look.
decisions: Channel pivot (2026-05-27): primary channels are now legal-industry outlets (ABA TECHSHOW, Lawyerist, Above the Law, IPWatchdog), not Product Hunt / Hacker News.
'Marketing-led only' model (2026-06-06): assumes no personal network and no warm intros — every tactic must work cold.
All public copy bound to a strict voice guide (first-person, plain, no AI-cliché words, no em dashes, every claim linked).
insights: Blunt diagnosis: the website's convert-the-visitor page is strong, so the failure is upstream — almost nobody arrives. A distribution problem, not a wording problem.
Credibility play: own an empty lane — 'private by architecture, not by promise.' No analyst currently champions local-first legal AI; open thought-leadership territory.
Near-term move: pitch the leading legal-tech journalist (Bob Ambrogi / LawSites) and apply to a conference startup showcase (ABA TECHSHOW Startup Alley).
Claim free directory listings lawyers use to vet tools (Clio App Directory, Capterra, G2, Software Advice) so Keepance 'exists' when checked — hold paid ads until a sales motion is proven.

sections.title: Sales
sections.now: There is no sales motion yet and no paying customers. The agreed plan is founder-led hand-selling, not self-serve signups or ads: pick one type of lawyer, run live 10–20 minute demos on the prospect's own real case file, and sell the outcome. Pricing, demo content, and objection scripts are prepared; what's missing is the selling activity itself, which is Jameson's to drive.
decisions: Sell by hand, not by funnel (2026-06-17): this market buys on peer trust, referrals, and live demos — hand-sell the first ~10 customers one at a time.
Recruit 3–5 'design-partner' lawyers on free pilots, to convert into the named testimonials future buyers require.
Win solo lawyers first, not firms: the firm tier needs trust credentials Keepance doesn't have yet.
Demo weighting: ~70% on the outcome (does the work, won't waive privilege or leak client data), ~30% on the privacy architecture.
insights: Four objections mapped for every demo: AI quality, IT setup burden, 'a DIY box is less secure,' and 'no security certification yet' — each with a prepared answer.

The strongest real pain signal in the whole record came from a financial advisor (Jameson's wife), NOT a litigator — so the chosen audience has technically never been validated. Flagged as a genuine risk.
Checkout snag for real sales: buy buttons still route through a shared store branded 'projelli,' so a lawyer sees an unrelated brand at checkout. Needs its own branded store before any real sale.

sections.title: Growth & Traction
sections.now: The honest weak point. By every measurable signal, Keepance is at idea-validation stage commercially despite a finished product. Verified directly from the systems (not estimated): zero real paying customers, zero genuine license activations (only Jameson's own tests), an empty firm-accounts database, ~225 website visitors in ten weeks (almost all direct), ~17 downloads of the latest version, a handful of 'buy' clicks ever, and empty email signup lists.
decisions: Name the reality plainly: 'a finished product meeting an untested market' — treat distribution + trust as the real problem.
Stop treating a sales problem as a build problem — the single biggest risk is polishing a product nobody has bought.
Define an explicit success/failure test (the kill-criterion) so 'keep building' can't quietly become the escape hatch from selling.
insights: The math is encouraging IF reach is solved: customers bring their own AI key, so cost per customer is near zero — even a modest number becomes real income.
Binding constraints, in order: (1) reach/distribution, (2) demo-to-close rate, (3) retention. Price is NOT the constraint.
A 'lifestyle business' income is reachable at a fairly small customer count; a 'real company' would need the firm tier (needs trust credentials) or a repeatable channel to hundreds of solo lawyers.
Structural risk: one non-developer operator, no sales experience yet, and a privacy angle that wins as a tiebreaker rather than a must-have.

sections.title: Competitive & Market
sections.now: Keepance occupies a genuinely unique spot: the only tool across legal, tax, consulting, and advisor AI offering a true local / nothing-leaves-your-machine option (competitor sweep, 2026-06-08). Incumbents (Clio Duo, Thomson Reuters CoCounsel, Microsoft Copilot, LexisNexis) are all cloud-based; the closest local rival (Elephas) is Mac-only with no legal features. But the market's default answer is 'cloud with strong assurances,' and lawyers are mostly moving toward the cloud, not away.
decisions: Keep a running competitor-watch log — the one event that most threatens Keepance is an incumbent adding a local or zero-egress option.
Frame the pitch as 'the most provably-private way to get AI's benefits,' NOT 'the cloud is unsafe' — the absolutist anti-cloud framing alienates the ~75% of lawyers already cloud-comfortable.
Keep competitor-comparison pages reconciled to current facts (CoCounsel pricing, LexisNexis's partial privacy feature).
insights: Encroachment to watch: LexisNexis 'Protégé' (Feb–May 2026) added customer-held encryption keys for big firms. Honest counter: it still routes data through their cloud; only a local model removes the trip entirely.
Well-funded rivals are mostly in adjacent categories (Jump $80M, Zocks $45M for advisors; Blue J $300M+ for tax) — they prove the space is hot but don't attack the local-first wedge.

Two citable legal angles strengthen the story: a Florida Bar opinion (local AI removes client-consent paperwork) and a 2026 federal ruling, U.S. v. Heppner (consumer-AI chats aren't privileged, so local = no waiver risk). Heppner is real — never delete it from materials.

Counter-pressure: 'bring your own key' is no longer unique to local-first, and a self-hosted box with no certification can be harder to defend to a cautious firm than hardened cloud — a real objection.

sections.title: Engineering
sections.now: The product is mature and genuinely solid — version 3.x, with signed auto-updating installers for Windows, Mac, and Linux and a deep feature set (Word editing with AI tracked-changes, ask-across-your-files-with-citations, email import/search, single sign-on, an encrypted vault, live multi-person co-editing). Driven hard as a real user on actual Windows hardware (2026-06-20), the headline feature — ask a question, get a correct answer with verified citations — worked end-to-end. A fresh-eyes structural review found the codebase sound.
decisions: Stop building net-new features; redirect effort to trust, honesty, and the email feature (the reorientation).

Fixed the product's self-contradictions (2026-06-17): a removed feature was still shown to paying customers, and a paid tier advertised credentials that don't exist yet — both corrected, with an automatic guard to prevent drift.
Customer-safety hardening: fixed places where a file-save or audit-log write could fail silently, and tightened the AI against attacker-controlled email content.
Latest fixes are written and tested but NOT yet released — cutting a new signed build is a slow, costly step that waits for Jameson's explicit go-ahead.
insights: New capability (this week): Claude can now drive the real desktop app on a Windows test machine like a user — far faster/cheaper bug-finding than the old hour-plus build-and-check loop.

Recent real bugs found and fixed live: privacy indicators that disagreed on the active AI provider; email that connected but never synced. One open gap (BUG-008): a stuck email sync shows no error, so it looks broken forever — fix planned.
Connectors to outside legal systems (Clio, iManage, Office add-ins) are blocked waiting on those vendors granting access — outside Keepance's control, deliberately deferred.
Multi-language support is partly wired and deferred — target customers are US firms.

sections.title: UX
sections.now: The app is reshaped around the law-practice identity with a clean, navy-railed layout organized by what a lawyer does (Matters, Search, Documents, Email, Workflows, Activity Log, Settings). A long polish pass (2026-06-16) tightened onboarding, account setup, and settings. A standout theme is making privacy visible and inspectable: an always-on indicator of where data is going, a plain-language 'Where your data is' map, and a one-click printable Confidentiality Report for the client file.
decisions: Trust as a visible product surface (2026-06-17): turned the privacy story from talking points into things a prospect can see and screenshot.
Hallucination guardrails in the experience: uncited answers carry a 'verify before relying on this' warning, and a one-click 'verify against source' flags fabricated or mismatched citations.
Honest onboarding: recommends the higher-quality bring-your-own-key mode as default, and presents max-privacy local mode honestly as 'more private, less capable for legal work.'
insights: Defensibility hinges on never quietly being wrong — a confidently-wrong answer is a malpractice/sanctions risk, so citation + verification is core, not cosmetic.
The email feature is the daily-use beachhead ('import your mail and actually find anything, with a citation, even when Outlook search fails') — make it a strong first-run, time-to-value moment.
A few UX papercuts logged (a failed search clears your typed question; a stuck email sync gives no feedback) — small but they hit first impressions.
Open idea: an opt-in, off-by-default 'design-partner' mode that learns from real usage without breaking the no-spying promise (structure only, never content).

sections.title: UI
sections.now: There's a real two-layer design system (built 2026-06-15): a foundation of shared style tokens (color, spacing, type, shadows) and a matching library of reusable building blocks (buttons, toggles, search fields, cards, badges). It covers the whole app — all seven main screens plus settings and the nav rail — so the same control looks and behaves identically everywhere. The theme is a polished light look (light background, dark text, navy accent).
decisions: Adopt the shared design system everywhere; stop using one-off hand-styled elements so the UI can't drift.
A fixed layout law for every screen: header, then one tools row (buttons → toggles → filters → search), then content.
Rebrand cleanup: replaced leftover 'projelli' branding (jellybean icon, installer images, window titles) with the correct Keepance shield identity — confirmed on real Windows.
insights: The design-system push was triggered by concrete inconsistencies (two differently-sized 'New' buttons; clashing filters) — fixing the system fixed the symptoms by construction.
Because Keepance sells trust, visual consistency is a trust signal — a sloppy interface reads to a lawyer as an unreliable product.
Open polish items are minor and non-blocking (a default-tab preference; some code-cleanliness debt).
Genuinely Windows-only visual checks (real Word interop, native folder picker, the auto-updater) still want a real-hardware spot-check.

sections.title: Finance & Metrics
sections.now: There is no real revenue and no live customer metrics — the honest state. The old financial plan (one-time price, a target with no customer-cost math) was retired as fiction; a new model was built (2026-06-17) around the real pricing. Pricing is per-seat ANNUAL: Solo $468 / Professional $948 / Firm $1,548 per seat (min 3 seats). A founding cohort gets 30% off for life; pre-3.0 one-time buyers are grandfathered forever.
decisions: Move to per-seat annual subscriptions in three tiers (2026-06-09) — well below specialized legal AI, at-or-above generic productivity AI.
Protect the local-first soul with a 'your files are always yours' guarantee — cancelling turns off AI features and updates, never your data.
Rebuild the financial model as a decision tool, not a forecast (2026-06-17): every conversion/churn/cost number is labeled an assumption to test.
Treat acquisition cost as time-bound, not cash-bound: spend is ~$0; the real cost is founder hours. Defer paid lead-gen until a sales motion is proven.
insights: The one durable bright spot: customers bring and pay for their own AI key, so cost per customer is near zero — roughly 95% gross margin, far above typical AI software. The only number in the model that isn't an assumption.

Rough scenario framing (assumptions, not forecasts): first ~10 customers ≈ $5–9K/yr (proves the thesis); a comfortable lifestyle level ≈ $60–90K/yr at a modest count; a 'real company' ($250K+) needs the firm tier or a repeatable channel.

The firm tier can't scale on 'trust me' — company-scale revenue depends on a trust moat (formed entity, a data-processing agreement, a SOC 2 certification, named references) that doesn't exist yet but is documented and ready to pursue when a deal demands it.
Re-run the whole model with real numbers only after the first ~10 customers; until then, don't steer by it.
